entry.title: [推荐] Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Jessica Croteau

Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. entry.title: [推荐] The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Caio Simoneti

This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. entry.title: [推荐] Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (3.0)

Karolin I. M. Tuncel、Tobias Müller

Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. Thesis Eleven · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (4.0)

Christian Fuchs

Nick Land is a British philosopher who has been leading the Dark Enlightenment movement. This paper examines the philosophical foundations of Land's right-wing trajectory and asks how the digital is integrated into his political economy and anti-humanist worldview. It situates Land within a broader context in which contemporary crises of neoliberal capitalism coincide with authoritarian and neo-reactionary currents often grouped under the label ‘Dark Enlightenment’. entry.title: [推荐] Individualism Without Individuality: Friedrich Hayek and the Neoliberal Citizen
entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (3.0)

Tal Tzur

Critics of neoliberalism increasingly examine its corrosive effects on democracy. Scholars often turn to Friedrich Hayek's political theory, arguing that it produces citizens who passively conform to spontaneous social orders. Yet insufficient attention has been paid to the normative conception of the human individual underlying his neoliberalism. This article demonstrates that Hayek's theory actively rejects individuality, understood as the cultivation and expression of one's distinct personal character. Individuality requires an experimental approach toward social action and critical reflection on whether social rules express one's character, yet such attitudes are systematically stifled in Hayek's account because they threaten the unequivocal obedience his spontaneous orders demand. entry.title: [必读] Adorno and the Kantian Sources of Ideology Critique
entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (11.35)

Antoine Athanassiadis

Social theorists in the Marxian tradition often interpret philosophical problems as reflections of social problems. This approach is central to Adorno's interpretation of Kant's epistemology. Adorno claims that the Critique of Pure Reason develops a concept of subjectivity that mirrors the “functionalization” of experience in capitalist societies. He retains that concept contradictory just as the social functionalism it ideologically reflects. In this paper I argue that Kant's concept of subjectivity is not contradictory and that Adorno must rely on it to articulate his critique of functionalism. Recognizing this Kantian debt implies not just acknowledging the Kantian sources of Adorno's model of ideology critique, but also revising central aspects of his social theory.

entry.title: [推荐] The Associationist 1848 and the Promise of Socialism
entry.content:
Modern Intellectual History · 1-26 · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (3.5)

John Mac Kilgore

For the American Fourierist movement known as Associationism, the European revolutions of 1848 represented the opening scene of a new world-historical struggle: “the Emancipation of Labor.” The momentous example of the French Revolution in particular pushed this group of cooperative labor reformers, often dismissed as “utopians,” to embrace the politics and persuasiveness of working-class agitation as a tactical means to reorganize the system of industry. I argue that the Associationists—sidelined, when not forgotten, in the existing scholarship of “the American 1848”—should be appreciated for placing socialism on the agenda as the promise of a future workers’ democracy in the United States. Not only that, but they came to view the US labor movement itself as a participant in the social and political transformations of the 1848 revolutions. This is the Associationist 1848.

This article challenges the reduction of blockchain to an institutional technology for lowering transaction costs by interpreting it as an autopoietic system of operational closure. Drawing on Francisco Varela's theory of biological autonomy and Cornelius Castoriadis’ account of political autonomy, it distinguishes between functional autonomy, understood as systemic self-maintenance, and political autonomy, understood as collective self-institution. The article argues that blockchain governance is marked by a rigidity paradox: the deterministic mechanisms that secure trustless coordination also risk foreclosing the indeterminacy required for democratic deliberation. M. Djemai Chebika、Rabah Kahli

This article traces a single, three-stage argument. It begins by documenting, with empirical precision, how digital platforms functioned as genuine instruments of horizontal mobilization during the North African uprisings of 2010–2012. It then analyses how those same platforms were rapidly incorporated into new and frequently more sophisticated architectures of social control, transforming what had been emancipatory tools into what Foucault would call dispositifs of docility. Finally, it asks what theoretical apparatus is adequate to comprehend this transition—and argues that the most productive framework is a deliberate synthesis of Foucault’s analytics of biopower and disciplinary normalization with Bauman’s diagnosis of liquid modernity. Werner Bonefeld

Contemporary critical theory elevates social norms to the status of positive knowledge and proclaims a politics of normative rightness to realise positive freedom and material equality in capitalist society. By accepting the positivity of norms, it fetishises them and prevents their denunciation, which alone exposes them. Based on the critical theories of Marx and Adorno, the article examines social norms as norms of a historically specific social content. Contemporary diagnoses of resurgent authoritarianism frequently attribute it to the political mobilization of fear, drawing on a long tradition that casts fear as the antithesis of freedom. This article argues that such a framework is conceptually inadequate in the face of climate breakdown. entry.title: [必读] The Ambivalence of Recognition in Sexual Subjectivity
entry.content:
Philosophy & Social Criticism · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (7.5)

Veerle van Wijngaarden

This paper addresses the problem of sexual misrecognition: some groups are excluded from being seen as sexually desirable or are hypersexualised. This shapes their sexual subjectivity – how they understand themselves as sexual agents. Despite widespread initiatives calling for recognition in the domain of sexuality, the need for sexual recognition has remained undertheorised in recognition theory. Building on debates on the ambivalence of recognition, I argue that sexuality has a uniquely complex relationship to recognition. While sexual recognition is necessary for subjectivity, it also reinforces subjection to power structures. Moreover, sexuality continually transgresses sociality and subjectivity itself. entry.title: [推荐] Collective Self-Rule and Comprehensive Participation: A Critique of Council Democracy
entry.content:
Philosophy & Social Criticism · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (3.0)

Erik van Ree

This article critically explores council democracy as a utopian state order, on the basis of anarchist and Marxist works from western Europe and the United States, post-World War 2. As a system of national government, council democracy cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises. Collective self-rule cannot put an end to domination/hierarchy/rule but will engender another variety of ‘democratic hierarchy’. Comprehensive citizen participation locks citizens in an overregulated ‘democratic bureaucracy’, and delivers no feasible, working formula of government. In a paradox, council democracy is likely greatly to reduce the share of the population participating in the country’s political process, thus carrying less rather than more democratic legitimacy than representative democracy.

entry.title: [必读] Social Inertia in Critical Theory
entry.content:
Philosophy & Social Criticism · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (13.2)

Bart Zantvoort

According to Adorno, all attempts to change society “immediately come up against the overwhelming force of inertia in the prevailing situation, and seem condemned to impotence.” This article explores the way the phenomenon of social and institutional inertia has been addressed in recent Critical Theory. It poses two central questions: firstly, what is social inertia, and what causes it? And secondly, how do we judge when institutions or social norms are “inert” or “obsolete”? It first briefly discusses the historical background of the problem of inertia, obsolescence and second nature in Hegel, Marx and the first generation of the Frankfurt School, and then discusses the central questions primarily with reference to recent work by Jaeggi and Menke and, to a lesser extent, Rosa and Von Redecker.

entry.title: [推荐] “Well grubbed, old mole!”: On Karl Marx in America by Andrew Hartman, University of Chicago Press, 2025
entry.content:
Thesis Eleven · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (6.0)

Gregory Jones-Katz

This review essay critically engages Andrew Hartman's Karl Marx in America , a reception history of three different classes of readings of Marx's writings in the United States. The essay's main contention is that Hartman's text, however unintentionally, seems to deviate from and thus challenges the anti-foundational principles that orient the genre of reception history. For, echoing Shakespeare's, Hegel's, and Marx's uses of the metaphor of the “Old Mole,” Hartman's own commitment to a labor-oriented version of “Marx”—from the three he charts in his topography of the Marx–America dialectic—works its way through Karl Marx in America , appearing at the end of text to subvert the groundless doctrines that guide reception histories.

entry.title: [必读] The Althusserian Transformation of Philosophy
entry.content:
Historical Materialism · 1-31 · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (10.05)

José Luis Moreno Pestaña

In this text I reconstruct the thinking behind Althusser’s work to define philosophy, which culminated in his 1976 presentation at the Granada conference. I start by exploring how philosophy exploits and reorganises other forms of knowledge and social practices by means of an analysis of Althusser’s works in the later part of the 1960s. Subsequently, I examine and outline the debates on how the mode of production affects the superstructure. I then turn to the positions of Althusser’s interlocutor at the Granada conference, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, who defended the idea that philosophy was affected by the mode of production. Finally, I examine the implications of the changes and innovations in Althusserian thought set out at the conference for the conception of philosophy.

This article reevaluates Walling as a neglected precursor to American Western Marxism, arguing that his 1912–1914 trilogy synthesized Marxist theory of his time and Deweyan pragmatism into a distinct “pragmatist conception of history.” Born into “aristocracy” yet radicalized, Walling's unique trajectory—as a co‐founder of the NAACP and critic of Second International orthodoxy—shaped his approach: a rejection of deterministic scientific history in favor of instrumental, presentist analysis limited to recent generations. Although his work anticipated Western Marxism's cultural turn and superstructural focus, it also embodied tensions between materialist foundations and pragmatist subjectivity. entry.title: [推荐] Virtue, wisdom, and inequality: A response to David Lay Williams’ The Greatest of All Plagues
entry.content:
European Journal of Political Theory · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (6.0)

Matthew W Maguire

This essay explores the distinctive humanist method through which The Greatest of All Plagues investigates the presence of economic inequality in the history of political thought. It then follows the various thinkers in the book—from Plato to Marx—and observes that a vocabulary of virtue and wisdom not only accompanies but often underwrites criticisms of inequality deep into the 19th century. In conclusion, Williams’ book implicitly allows his readers to perceive how virtue ethics and criticisms of inequality have only become separated in the late modern period. In the 21st century, their rapprochement will deepen and energize inquiries into virtue ethics and egalitarian approaches to political economy alike.

entry.title: [推荐] The Purview of the Particular: Power and Method in Foucaultian Genealogy
entry.content:
Constellations · Vol. 33 No. 3 331-342 · 推荐 (5.0)

Matt Kelley

If Foucault was anything, he was a particularist. And yet, if we are to find valuable tools in his method today, they must be able to assist our framing and analysis of non‐particular issues. By what means can Foucault's methods grasp trans‐contextual problems? I investigate this question by reconsidering the status of power in Foucault's genealogical method. Rather than acting as an object of inquiry, I propose that power operates as an orienting analytical category at the level of Foucault's method. I make the case that conceiving of power in this way facilitates a substantial degree of generalization of his approach that he and his commentators have frequently been wary of claiming. This rethinking of power and method establishes the capacity for Foucaultian methods to address contemporary systemic and global problems.
